questions.stem:
During our childhood in Goa, the baker used to be our friend, companion and guide. He used to come at least twice a day. Once, when he set out in the morning on his selling round, and then again, when he returned after emptying his huge basket. The jingling thud of his bamboo woke us up from sleep and we ran to meet and greet him. Why was it so? Was it for the love of the loaf? Not at all. The loaves were bought by some Paskine or Bastine, the maid-servant of the house! What we longed for were those bread-bangles which we chose carefully.

A student hears an elder say that the children of the house used to rush out whenever they heard the bamboo; according to the passage, what were they really waiting for? (A) The loaves that the maid-servant of the house had already bought (B) The bread-bangles that they chose carefully themselves (C) The sweet bread of special make that was kept for the elders (D) The hot tea that the baker carried along with the bread

answerScheme.modelAnswer: The bread-bangles that they chose carefully themselves

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Write an e-mail (100 words) to a friend in another city telling her about the Coorg you saw on your holiday — what the land is like, what it grows, and which months you would suggest for a visit.

markingPoints.description: Format: an e-mail with a subject line, a greeting, a body and a sign-off, within about 100 words (1)
Content: says that Coorg, or Kodagu, is the smallest district of Karnataka and is home to evergreen rainforests, spices and coffee plantations (1)
Content: gives the figure that evergreen rainforests cover thirty per cent of the district (1)
Content: says that during the monsoons it pours enough to keep many visitors away, and that the season of joy commences from September and continues till March (1)
Organisation, accuracy and expression: presents the details in a clear order and spells Coorg, Kodagu and Karnataka correctly (1)

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
Subject: The piece of heaven I saw in Coorg
Dear friend,
I have just come back from Coorg. Coorg, or Kodagu, is the smallest district of Karnataka, and it is home to evergreen rainforests, spices and coffee plantations. Evergreen rainforests cover thirty per cent of the district. Come in the season of joy: it commences from September and continues till March, and the weather is perfect. Avoid the monsoons, for then it pours enough to keep many visitors away. Coffee estates and colonial bungalows stand tucked under tree canopies in prime corners.
With love,
Your friend

questions.stem: Write a speech (100 words) to deliver in your school assembly telling the audience what you have learnt about the people of Coorg — the family they came from, the honour they have won, and the privilege they still enjoy.

Organisation: keeps the three points in a clear order — where the people came from, the honour they have won, and the privilege they still enjoy (1)

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
Good morning everyone,
Let me tell you three things about the people of Coorg. First, the fiercely independent people of Coorg are possibly of Greek or Arabic descent; as one story goes, a part of Alexander’s army moved south along the coast, settled there and married amongst the locals. Second, the Coorg Regiment is one of the most decorated in the Indian Army, and the first Chief of the Indian Army, General Cariappa, was a Coorgi. Third, even now Kodavus are the only people in India permitted to carry firearms without a licence. We should be proud of them.
Thank you.

questions.stem: One account says that after Goa’s liberation people said nostalgically that the Portuguese bread vanished with the Portuguese and the paders, but that the paders have managed to survive because they have perfected the art of door-to-door delivery service and pick up the knowledge of bread-making from traditions in the family. Another account says that those eaters of loaves might have vanished but the makers are still there, and that the age-old, time-tested furnaces still exist. Set out in steps where the two accounts agree, where they differ, and what each writer is doing.

markingPoints.description: Step 1: notes that both accounts are nostalgic about the good old Portuguese days and their famous loaves of bread (1)
Step 2: notes that both say the pader survived the Portuguese, the makers still being there and the paders having managed to survive (1)
Step 3: notes that both say the craft passes down in the family, the son carrying on the family profession and the knowledge being picked up from traditions in the family (1)
Step 4: sets out the difference on what vanished — the eaters of loaves in one account, the Portuguese bread in the other (1)
Step 5: sets out the difference in how the paders survived — the age-old, time-tested furnaces in one, the perfected art of door-to-door delivery in the other (1)
Step 6: says that the first account is personal and affectionate, while the second praises the unsung lives of the paders (1)

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
Step 1 — Both are nostalgic about the good old Portuguese days and their famous loaves of bread.
Step 2 — Both say the pader survived the Portuguese: the makers are still there, and the paders have managed to survive.
Step 3 — Both say the craft passes down in the family, from the father to the son.
Step 4 — They differ on what vanished: one says the eaters of loaves might have vanished, the other says the Portuguese bread vanished with the Portuguese.

Step 6 — The first is personal and affectionate; the second praises the unsung lives of the paders.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Set out in steps what the writer’s memories of the Goan village baker show about the rhythm of the day and how close the baker stood to every family in the village.

markingPoints.description: Step 1: gives the baker’s round — he came at least twice a day, once in the morning on his selling round and again after emptying his huge basket (1)
Step 2: says he greeted the lady of the house with “Good morning”, set his basket on the vertical bamboo and delivered the loaves to the servant (1)
Step 3: gives his dress — the kabai, a single-piece long frock reaching down to the knees (1)
Step 4: says the jingling thud of his bamboo woke the children, who ran to meet him and peeped into the basket (1)
Step 5: names what the children longed for — the bread-bangles they chose carefully, and sometimes sweet bread of special make (1)
Step 6: says he collected his bills at the end of the month and that the monthly accounts were recorded on some wall in pencil (1)

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
Step 1 — The baker came at least twice a day: in the morning on his selling round, and again after emptying his huge basket.
Step 2 — He greeted the lady of the house with “Good morning” and set his basket on the vertical bamboo; the loaves went to the servant.
Step 3 — He wore the kabai, a single-piece long frock reaching down to the knees.
Step 4 — The jingling thud of his bamboo woke the children; they ran to meet him and peeped into the basket.
Step 5 — What they longed for were the bread-bangles, which they chose carefully, and sometimes sweet bread of special make.
Step 6 — He collected his bills at the end of the month, and the accounts were recorded on some wall in pencil.
